draft.title: How dialogue builds character
card: Dialogue is the words characters speak to each other. It shows a reader what a character is like without the narrator saying so.
What a character says shows their personality and feelings. A character who admits taking a friend's pen by mistake and says sorry shows honesty and care.
How a character speaks also counts. Short, sharp replies can show anger. Long pauses and trailing words can show nerves or sadness.
Dialogue can shape how readers feel about a character. It can make readers like them, pity them or distrust them.
draft.remember: Both the words and the way they are spoken show who a character is.

a.q: In a story, Kai mutters "Fine. Whatever," and stares at the floor when his friend asks about his day. What does this dialogue most likely show?
opts: He is upset but does not want to talk about it
He is excited and wants to share his news
He is proud and wants to impress his friend
He is confused about what his friend asked
a.why: The short, flat replies and the stare at the floor show a character who is upset and hiding it. The excited option is wrong because excited speech would be eager and full, not clipped.
a.clue: Look at how short his replies are.

b.q: A character named Mr Voss keeps telling a new neighbour to trust him. He then urges her to sign a paper without reading it. What effect is this dialogue most likely to have on readers?
opts: It makes readers admire his honesty
b.why: He says to trust him, but he tells the neighbour not to read the paper. That is what a person with something to hide would do, so readers distrust him. Liking him is tempting because his words sound friendly, but his request works against them.
b.clue: Compare what he claims with what he asks the neighbour to do.

a.best: He is upset but does not want to talk about it
